analysis.one_liner: Bars corporate executives and directors from trading their company's stock before major news is officially filed.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote or a single cosponsor at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: When something big happens at a public company — a merger, an executive departure, bad earnings news — the company has up to four business days to file a Form 8-K, the official disclosure. During that gap, the company's own officers and directors know what happened but ordinary investors don't. This bill would direct the SEC to write rules forbidding those insiders from buying or selling their company's stock during the gap, closing a window that current law leaves open.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors who trade on the same information the public has. Today, a director can legally sell shares the moment bad news hits the company internally, before the disclosure is filed, at a price that hasn't yet reflected the news. The bill would force insiders to wait until everyone else can see what they see, and it specifically closes a loophole that lets insiders adopt 10b5-1 trading plans during the gap to shield those trades.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every reporting public company to adopt policies barring executive officers and directors from buying or selling company stock between the occurrence of a reportable event and the filing of the related Form 8-K, the official disclosure that can come up to four business days later.

Closes a known workaround: the SEC may not exempt trades made under a Rule 10b5-1 plan if the insider adopted that plan during the gap — so insiders cannot paper over a gap trade with a pre-set trading plan adopted after they already knew the news.
Also covers events a company has internally decided to disclose but has not yet filed, such as certain auditor changes or bankruptcies under items 7 and 8 of Form 8-K.

analysis.who_pays: Executive officers and directors of public companies, who lose a window in which they could trade on material information the public doesn't yet have. Public companies bear the modest cost of building and maintaining the required trading policies and controls. Financial firms like investment companies and registered advisers are exempted.

drawbacks.text: The trading gap is short — often a few days — and existing insider-trading and 10b5-1 rules already cover trades on material nonpublic information, so supporters of the status quo argue the bill adds compliance cost for a modest incremental gain.

The bill exempts investment companies and their advisers entirely, and exempts events already announced by press release, so insiders at some firms and some events keep trading freedom that others lose.
Because the bill mandates SEC rulemaking rather than a statutory ban, its real-world strength depends entirely on how the SEC writes and enforces the rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it eliminates a specific, short-lived advantage insiders hold over retail investors around major corporate events, including the 10b5-1 workaround. The costs are mostly compliance paperwork for companies and forgone trading flexibility for executives. It is a targeted fix, not a sweeping overhaul of insider trading law — which makes the lack of any cosponsor or committee action notable more than catastrophic.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on September 19, 2024, about two weeks before the end of the congressional session's legislative window.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, where it stayed; no markup, hearing, or floor action followed.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never received a vote in the House.
Bills not passed by both chambers expire when the Congress ends on January 3, 2025, so H.R. 9709 is dead and would need to be reintroduced to move again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public company executives and directors keep the ability to trade their company's stock during the gap between a major corporate event and its official disclosure, and companies avoid the cost of new trading-controls policies. No one in the investing public gained anything from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate insiders who trade during news gaps

for.name: Brad Sherman
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), bill sponsor and member of the Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Financial Services Committee; no colleagues joined him.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chair Patrick McHenry (R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member besides the sponsor took a position, so the partisan shape of support and opposition is unknown.

industries.note: They lose the ability to trade company stock during the days between a material corporate event and its official 8-K filing, including via 10b5-1 plans adopted in that window. Their gain under the status quo comes at the direct expense of investors trading on public information.
Companies must build and maintain policies and controls barring insider gap-trading, a real but modest compliance cost; cleaner disclosure timing can also improve market confidence.

industries.industry: Investment companies and registered investment advisers
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts them and their ethics-code requirements, so they face none of the new trading restrictions.
